newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine vice-president starts presidential bid.
newsitem.headline: Philippine vice-president starts presidential bid.

text.p: Philippine vice-president and one-time film action hero Joseph Estrada on Tuesday drew the battle lines for next year's presidential election, which will pit him against his boss's chosen successor.

One of the country's most popular politicians, Estrada resigned as head of the Presidential Anti-Crime Commission (PACC), the only job President Fidel Ramos has allowed him to hold other than the purely ceremonial role of vice-president.

"Having announced my bid for the presidency in next year's elections...I hereby tender my irrevocable resignation as chairman of the Presidential Anti-Crime Commission," he said in a letter delivered personally to Ramos.

Opposition leaders immediately hailed the resignation, which they said finally disassociated Estrada from a Ramos administration they claimed had failed to deal with the most critical problems of crime and unemployment.
"The resignation is long overdue. It will strengthen his credentials as a candidate of the opposition," said Ernesto Macedo, Senate president and head of one opposition party.
Estrada's move, which means he no longer sits in on Cabinet meetings, follows last week's announcement by Defence Secretary Renato de Villa that he would run in the May 1998 presidential race.
It is widely speculated that de Villa will carry with him the crucial endorsement of Ramos, who is barred by the constitution from standing for a second six-year term.
Estrada insisted his resignation was amicable and Ramos said in a news conference later that he had thanked the vice-president for his help in fighting crime.

Universally called "Erap" -- which spelled backwards in Tagalog, roughly translates as "pal" -- Estrada is seen as the man to beat, even if his huge popularity among the masses is not matched in a suspicious business community.
Earlier this year, a poll of businessmen by the influential Makati Business Club showed only three percent put him among their top candidates to run for president.
Number one was de Villa, followed by Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, an economist and one of the country's most popular politicians who recently threw her hat into the ring for next year's race.
Other contenders include Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo and House Speaker Jose de Venecia.
Estrada, who sports a 1950s-style quiff, has been criticised for womanising, heavy drinking -- both of which he says are sins of the past -- and for knowing nothing about the economy.

But he said he would continue the Ramos economic policies, which have seen the Philippine economy turn the corner to sustained growth after years of mismanagement, though he would concentrate on ending the plight of the poor.
"In all economic policies, the poverty alleviation is very important," he told reporters.
About a third of Filipinos live below the poverty line.
